title: Latency regression investigation: session-replay + metric anchors (working notes)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working note for a reproducible investigation pattern to diagnose latency regressions in tokenized inference paths. It leans on session-replay (reconstructing a user request path across services), a small set of metric anchors, and targeted span-level tracing to accelerate root cause discovery.

Intended audience:
- Oncall engineers and SREs responding to latency SLO breaches
- Product/feature owners triaging repeated regressions
- Dashboard owners who will add snippets and anchors to the main Investigations dashboard

Why this approach?
- Many existing playbooks assume a single faulty service; inference stacks are multi-stage (api gateway -> preprocessor -> serving runtime -> kv-cache -> model shards).
- Session-replay synthesizes the single request timeline across these stages so we can see which stage amplified latency variance.
- Metric anchors are a compact set of signals that are cheap to query and correlate with spans. Anchors reduce blind triage time.

Definitions (quick):
- session-replay: reconstructing the full event sequence for a request id (ingress timestamp, routing decision, batch join, model token start/end).
- metric anchor: a single aggregated metric (or dimensioned timeseries) that reliably moves when a particular subsystem changes (e.g., batch_size_histogram, kv_cache_hit_rate).
- span anchor: a recommended span name and attributes to prioritize in traces (e.g., span=serve.kv_lookup, attr=cache_hit=true).

Anchor list (minimal, queried first):
1) request.p99_latency_ms --- global user-facing latency SLI (ingress->final-response).
2) batch.join_ms.p95_by_model --- how long requests wait to form a batch (per-model).
3) kv_cache.hit_rate_5m --- moving window cache hit rate.
4) server.token_gen_p95_ms --- model token generation time (region+model).
5) connection.queue_depth --- runtime inbound queue depth (per-node).
6) cpu_utilization.gpu_percent_95 --- GPU utilization tail.
7) storage.read_latency_ms.p95 --- external weight fetch/embedding table reads.

Span anchors to prioritize in traces:
- http.ingress (attrs: route, api_key_version)
- preproc.tokenizer (attrs: tokens_in)
- batch.join (attrs: model, batch_size)
- serve.kv_lookup (attrs: cache_hit, key_count)
- runtime.infer (attrs: model_variant, seq_len, quantized=true/false)
- streaming.write (attrs: chunk_count, bytes)

Investigation steps (ordered, aim for 10–20 minutes to narrow to subsystem):
Step 0 — get context (1–2 min):
- Check pager alert and the SLO window (time range). Note impacted routes/models/customer tiers.
- Capture a sample request id (if alert contains one) or pick a high-latency trace id from the error/trace sampling UI.

Step 1 — quick anchor sweep (2–4 min):
- Query anchors at the alert time +/- 5m. Use prebuilt dashboard panels for p95/p99 and short histograms.
- Look for deviations: e.g., elevated batch.join_ms.p95_by_model or drop in kv_cache.hit_rate_5m.
- If a single anchor spikes (e.g., batch join), go to the relevant subsystem drilldown.

Step 2 — session-replay reconstruction (3–6 min):
- Reconstruct timestamps per stage using trace spans or request logs. Build (or use) the lightweight session-replay UI/SQL that joins logs by request_id and orders events.
- Visual cues to prefer: long idle gap before a span (waiting), long single span duration (processing), or repeated retries.
- If session shows long idle before batch.join, likely scheduling/scale issue; if long runtime.infer, likely model performance or hardware saturation.

Step 3 — trace sampling and focused spans (2–5 min):
- Increase trace sampling for the implicated route/model (temporary) to collect more examples.
- Pull a set of traces and look for span attributes that correlate with slow traces: seq_len, quantized flag, model_variant, cache_hit=false.

Step 4 — correlate infra signals (2–5 min):
- Check node-level metrics (cpu/gpu/top processes), queue_depth per instance, and scaling events (autoscaler logs).
- Confirm whether the pattern is single-node or fleet-wide. Single-node noisy neighbor suggests isolate/replace instance; fleet-wide suggests model/kernel change.

Step 5 — test hypotheses (5–15 min):
- If batchization: simulate production request shape and measure batch join under load on canary nodes.
- If kv cache: run a targeted cache warmup and measure effect on p95/p99.
- If model runtime: compare recent model or kernel rollouts (check rollout tag in runtime.infer spans).

Typical root causes and fingerprints:
- Increased batch.join_ms with no change in runtime.infer -> scheduling pressure (too small fleet, autoscaler lag, or misconfigured latency target).
- Drop in kv_cache.hit_rate + runtime.infer p99 up -> cold cache leading to heavier model runs.
- Single model_variant shows slow runtime.infer while others fine -> model quantization or kernel change.
- GPU utilization high but queue_depth also high -> undersized capacity or slow kernel.

Dashboard notes (what to add to Investigations dashboard):
- Compact anchor panel (those 6 anchors) with a time-range selector and model filter.
- Session-replay sparkline: per-request timeline waterfall for the last N traces (selectable).
- Top 5 span attributes correlated with latency (auto-inferred via chi-square or mutual information).
- A “recent rollout” timeline with links to GitHub PRs and rollout ids observed in spans.

Tracing instrumentation suggestions (small, high-leverage):
- Ensure batch.join emits batch_size and model; annotate whether join waited for a slot vs. batching window expiry.
- runtime.infer must include model_variant, seq_len, and quantization level as attributes.
- Tag any fallback or retry spans with fallback_reason and previous_latency_ms.
- Emit node_id for runtime spans to correlate with instance-level logs.

Playbook templates (alert -> ticket fields):
- Impacted routes/models: [list]
- Anchor deviations observed: [list]
- Top suspect subsystem: [serving/batching/kv/cache/network/storage]
- Action taken: [trace sampling increased, node replaced, rollback PR tagged]
- Next steps: [scale up, rollout revert, add dashboard anchor, follow-up postmortem]

Short-term mitigations (fast options):
- Enable fallback models with lower seq_len if runtime.infer spikes.
- Throttle non-critical routes to protect higher tier customers.
- Warm cache via synthetic warmers for hot keys.

Longer-term changes to reduce investigation time:
- Auto-attach the nearest session-replay to any latency alert (goal: surface one coherent request timeline in pager message).
- Expand anchor set to include tail percentiles per-customer tier and per-model.
- Automate correlation: when a span attr value (e.g., model_variant=abc-v2) explains >60% of slow traces, inject that hypothesis natively into the alert.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How often do we see cross-model interference due to shared GPU memory? Need to instrument device-level memory allocation per job.
- Can we add a lightweight binary fingerprint for model kernels emitted in spans so we can quickly compare kernel versions?
- Is the session-replay UI performant for ranges with thousands of traces? (Consider sampling and summarization.)

Quick references (queries/snippets):
- p95 join per model: SELECT model, percentile(batch_join_ms, 95) FROM batches WHERE ts BETWEEN t0 AND t1 GROUP BY model
- kv hit-rate: rate(sum(kv_hits) / sum(kv_requests))[5m]
- slow traces by attr: SELECT trace_id, duration_ms, attrs FROM traces WHERE duration_ms > threshold AND attrs.model = 'X' LIMIT 50

Notes on tone: keep defaults conservative when suggesting mitigations; prefer replacing nodes or increasing sampling rather than wide rollbacks.

Next steps for this doc:
- Merge into Observability Playbooks with a compact checklist widget. (Assigned: Marcus)
- Add example session-replay screenshot to the dashboard notes (Assigned: Priya).
- Prototype automated hypothesis injection on alert (Spike ticket pending).

End of working notes.

-- AM (Alicia Mendez), 2026-02-15
